Start here

Emberwake is a 2D pixel-art open-world game. Dig, build, craft and fight across an endless world and seven other worlds beneath and above it, alone or with up to three friends. Fighting is about timing, not mashing. The FFA Arcade has ten weapon-focused arenas for solo practice with three echo bots or private matches by code. The Ashfall Trials and the Wilds are separate survival arenas. No internet is needed to play alone.

What's in the folder

In the folderWhat it is
Emberwake.appthe game as a Mac app: double-click it to play
Emberwake.htmlthe same game for any computer: double-click it to play in your web browser
Emberwake Guide.htmlthis guide
Sourceeverything for changing the game: its code, this guide's text, the Mac app's parts, and the tests

The app and the HTML file each work on their own, so you can move either one anywhere (the app into Applications, the HTML file onto a USB stick).

On a Mac

Drag Emberwake.app into your Applications folder and double-click it. The game opens in its own window with its own icon and menu, using the web engine built into macOS, so you don't need a browser.

The first time, macOS warns that it can't check the app, because it isn't from the App Store or a registered developer. To open it anyway:

  • macOS 15 Sequoia and later: double-click the app and click Done. Then open System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down, and click Open Anyway next to Emberwake.
  • Earlier macOS: right-click (or Control-click) the app, choose Open, then click Open again.
  • Or, in Terminal: xattr -cr /Applications/Emberwake.app

After that it opens with a normal double-click. Cmd+Q quits, Ctrl+Cmd+F switches full screen on and off, and closing the window quits too.

On any other computer

Double-click Emberwake.html to play in your web browser (Chrome, Safari, Edge or Firefox), on Windows, Linux, a Chromebook or a Mac.

It plays in the browser of a phone or a tablet too. Touch controls appear by themselves (see Controls: On a phone or tablet).

Signing in

The game opens on the ACCOUNTS board. The first time, choose + CREATE ACCOUNT: type a name and a password (eight characters or more, typed twice), pick a look and a hat, and you are in. After that, SELECT your account, type its password and choose LOG IN.

  • An account lives in this browser (or in the app). Nothing is sent anywhere, so there is nobody to ask if you forget the password.
  • Your worlds are yours. Each account has its own list of worlds. Worlds made before there were accounts go to the first account made.
  • Above the WORLDS board you see your account's name and SIGN OUT. Click the name to come back to the ACCOUNTS board, where CHANGE LOOK lets you choose another look or hat, and + CREATE ACCOUNT makes one for somebody else who plays here.

Your saves

Saves stay on the computer you play on, with the account that made them. The app and each browser keep their own accounts and their own saves.

To take a world from the app to a browser, or to another computer, choose COPY next to the world in your world list. On the other side, choose PASTE A WORLD.

Everyone you play with needs this same version of the game. When you get a new version, send your friends the new Emberwake.html (or the app) too.

Controls

KeyWhat it does
A / Dmove
Space or Wjump (hold S to drop through bridges)
Shiftdodge (dodge through a hit at the last moment, then strike back: a riposte)
Left mousea light blow. Strike again when your weapon glints, not before (see Fighting: the beat). Holding it down does not attack. Clicking a creature always punches it, whatever you hold
Right mouse or Qa heavy blow: spends your tempo for a harder hit (hold to charge); also opens doors
Vchange weapon style (five per weapon, unlocked by training)
Xswap to your off-hand weapon (pairs make combo finishers)
1 to 0, mouse wheelhotbar
Eyour pack, what you wear, and crafting by hand
Bthe recipe book: every bench, what it is for and what it makes
Gdrop one of what you hold (Shift+G drops the whole stack)
Ftalk, use a bench, sleep, plant, take honey, wake a guardian with its offering, touch a rift or an echo stone
Hquick heal
Jjournal: leads, lore, echoes, bestiary
Mmap (once you have drawn one; in the battle royale, the island)
Kknapping (optional: stone heads can also be made by hand from flint)
Cforms (your moves)
R / Tthrow / switch sidearm
Osound on or off
P or Escmenu (PLAY TOGETHER is in here). In the Wilds P offers, accepts and leaves a pact, and only Esc opens the menu
Enterchat, when playing with friends

Your pack

Press E. Drag a stack to move it, drag one out of the pack to drop it, and shift-click to send a stack between the hotbar and the pack. Right-click splits a stack. Chests, crates, barrels and strongboxes have TAKE ALL and STORE ALL (store all keeps your hotbar as it is).

Under the pack, WORN holds your armour, your off-hand weapon and your trinkets. Right-click armour or a trinket in your pack to put it on, or drop it on its slot. The BOOK button (or B) opens the recipe book.

Your hands

Anything you only carry (ore, bars, rope, keys, sidearms) leaves your fists free. Click and you punch: jab, cross, hook, uppercut. Aim up for an uppercut, aim down or hold S for a low kick, and use the right mouse button for a haymaker.

Blocks, food and other usable things still do their job when you click empty space, but a click on a creature is always a punch. Tools swing where you point and hit creatures as well as rock. Pointing at ground within reach with empty hands digs by hand.

On a phone or tablet

Touch controls appear by themselves, whichever way up you hold it. With a mouse and keys they never show.

  • The stick moves you. Pull it down to drop through a bridge or aim low. JUMP, DASH, USE, LIGHT and HEAVY are the buttons around it. DASH is the dodge (the Shift key). USE is the F key, and you can hold it.
  • LIGHT and HEAVY strike at whoever is in front of you. The beat is the same as with a mouse: tap again when your weapon glints. Holding a button down does not attack again.
  • Touch the world to dig, gather or strike exactly there. Tap the hotbar to change what you hold.
  • PACK opens your pack and crafting: tap a recipe to make it, slide a finger to scroll, CLOSE to go back. HEAL is a quick heal, MAP the map (once you have drawn one) and MENU the menu.
  • CHAT shows when friends are in your world.
  • PACT shows in a Wilds match: it offers and accepts a pact, and tapped twice leaves it.
  • Tap a name, a seed, a game code or an account field to type in it: your keyboard comes up.

The menu (Esc)

  • Controls: SIMPLE (the default). Only where you aim (up, straight, down) and holding S choose your attack, so you never lunge or dash across the screen by surprise. FULL brings back the extra forms tied to the movement keys and how far away the cursor is (the forms page, C, greys them out in SIMPLE).
  • Difficulty: EASY (the default): you take 30% less damage, heal twice as fast, get hungry more slowly, and the timing of your blows is generous. NORMAL is the original balance. HARD: 25% more damage taken, slower healing, faster hunger.
  • Crafting: SIMPLE (the default). At a station you click what you want and it is made after a short bar fills (shift-click makes five). Fires and kilns work whenever they have fuel, and light themselves from your sticks or logs; food never burns. HANDS-ON brings back the station games (sawing, the potter's wheel, the bellows, the anvil...), heat and the kiln's damper, and food that chars if you forget it.
  • FX: FULL (the default): the glow of fires and blades, the colour each land and season gives the air, the morning mist, the embers your Waker trails at a run. FX: PLAIN turns those off; try it if the game stutters on an older machine.
  • FPS MODE: OFF (the default). Turn it on to stop particle effects and hide the lesser parts of the HUD, for a cleaner and smoother view. Health, stamina, the hotbar, boss bars and a clear aiming cross stay. The game stays side-on (it is not a first-person view), and the world, the fighting and play with friends are the same.

The menu also shows the day and the season, and what kind of world this one is (its three traits).

All five are remembered on this computer.

How to play

You wake with nothing. Everything after that is up to you: there is no wrong order, and nothing forces you along.

Crafting

Open your pack (E). The BY HAND list shows everything you can make anywhere. Green lines you can make now, and each ingredient shows what you have against what it needs (for example 2/3 Plant Fiber). Hover a line to see it spelled out, and click to make it. The things you can almost make come first.

Everything else is made at benches you build and place. Each bench has one job, so you always know where to go. Stand next to one and press F: its list works the same way, and a bench with a long list has a SHOW button (weapons, tools, armour...) and a CAN MAKE switch. Every item's tooltip says where it is made, and the recipe book (B) lists every bench, what it is for, how to build it, and everything it makes.

At the Workbench, choose SHOW: ARMOUR to see every set together. Armour takes fewer materials than it did, and all of it is made there: no separate stand, and no anvil of the armour's rank.

BenchWhat it is for
Workbenchwoodwork and armour: planks, doors, ladders, wooden and bone weapons, most other benches, and every piece of armour (metal and other-world sets too)
Carpenter's Tablefurniture and things to place: crates, barrels, beds, tables, planters, signposts, lamps
Anvilmetal weapons and tools. Stone anvil: copper and bronze. Iron anvil: iron and steel. Slagforge: the metals of the other worlds
Armourer's Standan older bench, kept so that worlds which have one stay as they are. It has nothing left to make: armour is made at the Workbench
Tinker's Tablegadgets you carry (lanterns, glider, climbing claws, compass, gauges), traps and the ember ballista
Jeweller's Benchtrinkets you wear: rings, charms and amulets
Hearth Ovenhot meals that give a boon for a few minutes
Cauldronbrews: salves, tonics, antidotes, flasks to throw
Offering Altarthe offerings that wake the guardians, the lamps that call the sky, and the keys between worlds
Mason's Benchcut stone: blocks, walls, statues, fountains, the stone anvil and the oven

The workshops turn raw things into materials: the kiln (brick, glass, charcoal, pots), the bloomery (ore into bars), the loom (cloth, rugs, banners, bags), the quern (ore, powder, flour), the potter's wheel, the drying rack, the sieve and the campfire.

Trinkets and meals

Trinkets work while you wear them. You start with two trinket slots; the first time you beat the Ashen Warden, Vesper, the Forge-Keeper and the Slag Tyrant, each opens one more (six in all). A few of the many: the Quickstep Ring (walk faster), the Miner's Charm (dig faster), the Ashen Veil (a wider window for a perfect dodge), the Counter Sigil (counters hit harder), the Rhythm Bead (follow-ups pay more), the Thorn Ring, the Fang Necklace (blows drink a little life), the Ember Heart (slow healing). Each guardian also leaves a trophy trinket of its own.

Meals from the Hearth Oven fill you up and give one boon for a few minutes: an Emberberry Pie makes you QUICK, a Hunter's Pie HEARTY, a Honey Cake SWEET (stamina), a Fire Roast WARM, a Glowcap Stew GLOWING, Spiced Jerky FIERCE, a Miner's Stew DELVING, and the Waker's Feast does several at once. The last meal you ate is the one that counts. Flour comes from reeds at the quern; honey from a beehive.

Eating and brews

Eating takes a moment. Your Waker stops to lift the food, a bite is quick, and a meal or a drink takes a little longer. A blow interrupts it, and you keep the food. So eat before the fight or step out of it first.

Brews are drinks that change a fight for a short while. Each rank of brew needs a better vessel:

BrewMade atWhat it does
Quickstep Brewa Cauldronyou move more than a quarter faster for 40 seconds
Emberheart Brewa Brewer's Stand (built at a Workbench)your blows hit about a fifth harder for 30 seconds
Doublesoul Draughta Moon Cauldron (built at a Mason's Bench, around a cauldron)calls a mirror of you for 40 seconds

Only one of the first two burns in you at a time: drink another and it takes the place of the first. The time left shows with your boons.

The mirror stands up beside you with the weapon you hold. It repeats your last few steps, then fights with a mind of its own. It hits more lightly than you do and can be beaten down. You can have one mirror at a time, and it will not come again until a minute after you called it: it stays forty seconds, so that is twenty seconds after it goes home.

The brews want things from the two new lands (see No two worlds alike): a willow feather for Quickstep, willow eggs for Emberheart, a moonseed for the Doublesoul Draught. Two eggs, salt and berries at the Hearth Oven make a Willow Omelet, a HEARTY meal. The recipe book (B) has every recipe.

Feathers can be had in any world: besides the willow hen, the galewisp that walks in a thunderstorm leaves them. Eggs and moonseed cannot. Eggs come only from the willow hen and a moonseed only from the moss deer, and those two live only in the Mosswood and the Willowmere. These two lands are in worlds forged in this version, and in worlds brought over from the version that had accounts. An older world has neither land, so the Emberheart Brew, the Doublesoul Draught and the Willow Omelet cannot be made there: do not hunt for eggs or moonseed in it.

Things to place

  • Storage: crates (10 stacks), barrels (20) and strongboxes (30), as well as chests.
  • A bed: you wake there after a fall. Sleep in it (F) to pass the night and wake rested (you heal for a while). A table, a chair and a light nearby make it cosy, and the rest lasts twice as long.
  • Planter boxes: plant berries, reeds, fibre, mushrooms or glowcaps, and come back when it's ripe. Mushrooms like the dark; the rest like the sun.
  • Beehives make honey, faster near flowers and berry bushes. Fountains fill your empty jugs, and heal you while you rest beside them. Braziers keep the cold off.
  • Defences: spike traps and snares for whatever walks over them, the ember ballista that shoots creatures coming close, and a warning bell that rings when they do.
  • Signposts show on your map. A weapon rack shows off a weapon. Lamp posts, candles and chandeliers light a room; tables, chairs, bookshelves (read them!), rugs, banners, fences, statues, flower pots, stained glass, polished stone, mosaic, roof tiles and mossy brick make it a home.
  • Gadgets you carry work from anywhere in your pack: the depth gauge, the pocket watch (the time, and how long until dark) and the ore seeker (ore near you glints).

Fighting: the beat

A fight has a pulse, and you win by keeping it. Hammering the mouse button loses. Holding it down does nothing at all.

  • The glint. After every blow your weapon glints (your Waker catches the light too, and there is a soft tick). Strike again on the glint and the chain goes on. Right on it is CRISP: a little more damage and some stamina back.
  • Rushed. Strike before the glint and the blow in your hand is RUSHED: weaker, much slower to recover from, and the chain starts over. This is what happens to anyone who mashes.
  • Tempo. Every blow struck in time lights an ember (up to five; they circle your Waker and show above the hotbar). Each ember makes your blows hit harder. Embers fade if you stop landing blows, and you lose them when you are hit, when you rush, or when you swing at nothing.
  • Spending it. A heavy blow (right mouse) takes every ember with it and hits far harder for each one. At five embers it is a CRESCENDO. Blades and fists get the most from this.
  • Biting. A lone light blow hurts a sturdy foe but does not stop it: it keeps coming. Blows in time, heavy blows and clean blows bite: the foe flinches. So one click at a time is the weakest way to fight, and a timed chain is the strongest.
  • Clean hits. Where the weapon lands matters. A blade or a chain: the outer half. A pike: the point, at full reach (too close and it is JAMMED). Fangs: in the back. A maul: the end of the swing. Fists: a punch that beats their wind-up. An arrow: the HEAD.
  • Their guard. Bigger foes have a guard (a thin amber bar under their health once you test it). Blows that bite wear it down; when it BREAKS they reel for a moment and everything hurts them more. Guardians have one too.
  • Sunder. A heavy blow on a foe whose guard is broken is a SUNDER: half again as hard, and it gives you back stamina and two embers. It works once each time the guard breaks. Break them, then finish it.
  • Their blows. A foe shows ! over its head before it strikes. Answer it: dodge (Shift) through the blow and strike back for a riposte, or CLASH: time a swing of your own so it meets theirs, and theirs is turned aside.
  • The answer. For a second after a clash, your next blow is the ANSWER: it hits a quarter harder and always bites.
  • Perfect release. Hold the heavy button to charge a blow, and let go just as it flashes: a PERFECT RELEASE, a fifth harder. Hold on too long and it is only a charged blow.
  • Caught. Being hit while you wind up, or after you rush, hurts a quarter more and takes all your embers.
  • Stamina. A rushed blow and a swing at nothing both cost stamina, so mashing leaves you with no wind to dodge or strike heavy.
  • Warded foes. Now and then a foe carries a shield (you can see it, and its name says Warded). Plain blows from the front glance off. A heavy blow, a clean one or a critical one gets through, and so does anything from behind: dodge through it and turn. Break its guard and the shield drops while it reels.

Each kind of weapon keeps the beat its own way. The forms page (C) says how, under In time:

WeaponIn time
Bladesheavy blows spend embers best
Pikesa clean point lights two embers
Fangsembers fade slowly
Maulsa heavy blow that lands keeps two embers
Bowsa head shot lights two embers
Chainsthe glint lasts longer
Fistsa wider moment to clash

How hard things hit. Each metal is about a fifth better than the one before it, all the way up. For the same metal, a slow weapon hits hardest and a long one least, but used well they all end up within reach of each other: pick the one whose rhythm you like. Tools are not weapons: a tapped pick or axe does about half what a sword of the same metal does, and a wound-up swing (hold the right button) nearly as much as one.

The practice post in the village teaches all of this: press F at it with a weapon in hand. The journal (J) keeps a page called The Beat of a Fight. On EASY the timing is generous; NORMAL and HARD tighten it.

Keeping your run

A blow or a dodge no longer stops you dead. Hold a direction through a swing and you keep most of your run, so you can strike on the way past and carry on. A dodge flows back into a run the same way. Take your hands off the keys and you glide to a stop. Strike behind you while you back away and you do not turn round. A blow thrown standing still is exactly as it was.

Styles, set-ups and arts

Each kind of weapon (blades, pikes, fangs, mauls, bows, chains, fists) has its own fighting style, and you learn it by using it. A new weapon family starts at BASICS (the plain combo, the heavy blow, the air combo and the counter). Keep fighting with it and it grows to FOOTWORK (sweeps, rising strikes, dives), then FLOW and MASTERY (dashes, charged and aimed heavies). The forms page (C) shows what each step teaches.

Every attack sets up the next. A sweep knocks a foe DOWN: hit a downed foe with a heavy blow or from above and it CRUSHES. Launch a foe and your air blows JUGGLE it, then a dive SPIKES it. Lunges and dashes leave a foe OPEN for a heavy blow that BREAKS it. Thrusts SKEWER a pinned, hooked or reeled foe. Each family leans on some of these more than others.

A perfect dodge (dodge just as a blow lands) opens a counter: attack straight away for a riposte, aim up for a rising counter, hold S for a sweeping one, or use the heavy button for a reversal; in the air, a diving one.

Arts. The better weapons (steel and up, and the old named weapons) each hide an art: a big, special move. Keep landing blows with one and it teaches you; then hold the right mouse button to call it.

The road ahead

The road looks roughly like this:

  1. The Waking Lands. Gather by hand, knap flint, build a bench, a kiln, a bloomery and an anvil. Work your way through copper and bronze. Three guardians each keep one of the fallen embers: the Ashen Warden, Vesper at the Mirror Court, and the Forge-Keeper in the Drowned Forge. The world is endless in both directions and forms around you as you travel. Each guardian wakes for an offering (see The guardians below).
  2. The Furnace Gate. With all three embers the gate opens onto the Kiln Heart, a rift into Cinderdeep.
  3. Cinderdeep. A molten world under everything. Mine cinderite (it needs an embersteel pick). Build a Slagforge at an iron anvil (slagrock, charglass, embersteel, cinderite): it works every new tier. Wake the Slag Tyrant at the altar in its caldera with a Cinder Offering. Charge it into the caldera wall and it staggers.
  4. The Ember Moon. After you have been to Cinderdeep, some nights the moon rises red and moonwretches drip moon wax. Make a Moon Lantern from it at the Offering Altar and call the moon yourself: then, late in the night, the Pale Shepherd walks. Its bell lets you call the Ember Moon whenever you like.
  5. The Rootward Key (Offering Altar: Tyrant's Core, 5 cinderite bars, 3 moon wax). Touch it to any rift to open the Rootdark: dark, wet, lit by fungus. Gloom ore needs a cinderite pick; gloomsteel needs spore dust. The Rootmother wakes for a Root Offering and is rooted in place: strike her tendrils, or wait for her to bloom.
  6. Starfall and the Eclipse. After the Rootdark, some nights shed starshards you can catch where they land. After the Rootmother falls, some days go dark at noon and Umbral Knights walk (their shields face you: strike after they swing).
  7. The Prism Key (Offering Altar: Heartseed, 5 gloomsteel bars, 4 starshards, 2 umbral shards) opens the Glass Expanse: islands of a broken sky over nothing. Glass walkways join the islands and updrafts lift you to the high ones. Fall into the void and it throws you back, hurt. The Prism Matriarch wakes for a Prism Offering and keeps her spire: step out of the red line before it turns white.
  8. Her heart makes the Starsplitter, or can be drunk for good.

Each of the four new guardians (the Tyrant, the Rootmother, the Matriarch and the Shepherd) makes you permanently tougher the first time you beat it. Each world has its own weather too: eruptions in Cinderdeep, spore blooms in the Rootdark, shatterstorms in the Expanse. The Waking Lands get Ashfall and the Long Fog, each with creatures that only walk then.

Waygates. Once you have cinderite you can forge a Waygate at a Slagforge and place it anywhere, so you don't have to walk back to the Furnace Gate.

The guardians

The guardians answer offerings, not chance. Build an Offering Altar (at a Mason's Bench). Each offering is made from things you gather and something the guardian before it left behind:

GuardianWhereOfferingIt leaves
Ashen Wardenthe shrineAshen Offering: 6 charcoal, 3 copper bars, 4 bone, 2 resinthe first ember, Warden's Sigils (the Iron Anvil needs one, so iron and steel come after the Warden)
Vesperthe mirrorMirror Offering: 4 glass, 2 bronze bars, 3 salt, a Warden's Sigilthe second ember, Glass Sigils
Forge-Keeperits anvilForge Offering: 5 iron bars, 4 bronze bars, 8 coal, a Glass Sigilthe third ember, Keeper's Sigils
Slag TyrantCinderdeep's altarCinder Offering: 10 slagrock, 4 charglass, 3 cinderite ore, a Keeper's Sigilits core (the Rootward Key), slag hearts
Rootmotherthe Rootdark's altarRoot Offering: 10 rootwood, 6 capflesh, 4 gloom ore, a slag heartits seed (the Prism Key), moth wax
Prism Matriarchthe Glass Expanse's altarPrism Offering: 10 shardglass, 8 palestone, 4 prism ore, 2 moth waxher heart

Each guardian also leaves a trophy trinket the first time, and the first four each open a trinket slot. You can wake any of them again with another offering.

Above ground, and the four worlds past the floors

The surface matters as much as the deep. Sunstone shows in high rock only by daylight. Skyiron lies where stars came down (craters). Sunbloom opens by day and moonpetal by night. Hawks round the peaks drop skyfeathers. Sun shrines on hilltops trade sunstone for health at midday, and observatories hold old gears, storm glass and a telescope that marks the four gates on your map. In a thunderstorm, a lightning rod you have raised turns strikes into storm glass; a Storm Bell calls a storm when you want one.

Past the three floors there are four more worlds. Each has a gate on the surface, a key made from the last guardian's prize and from things that only the surface gives, three lands of its own, a better forge, its own steel and weapons, a new art for every weapon family, and a guardian:

WorldIts gateWhat is different thereIts forge and steelIts guardian
The Long Winterthe Frost Gate, on a peak in the cold country (Frost Key)the cold: stay near fire or wear frostfurRime Forge, rimesteel (chills, then shatters)the Winter Stag
The Stopped Hourthe Stopped Clocktower (Hour Key)spring pads, moving belts, and a great chime that stills everything but youEscapement, hourbrass (blows echo a moment later)the Horologist, who rewinds its own wounds
The Stormheadthe Stormspire, which opens only in a thunderstorm (Storm Key)wind, and lightning that hunts youThunder Anvil, stormsteel (arcs between foes)the Stormwright
The Outsidethe Ringstair (the Dawnring)the dark: carry light or be foundDawn Anvil, dawnsteel (burns the hollow)the Hollow King

Every guardian in the game leaves a fragment the first time it falls. All ten, with stormsteel and sunstone, forge the Dawnring at a Thunder Anvil. It opens the Ringstair; at the Cold Hearth in the Outside, with an Ember Offering, it calls the Hollow King. What happens after is the end of the story, and you can keep playing.

Each guardian's offering needs things from several worlds and from the surface, so no guardian can be woken by staying in one place. The journal's leads (J) say exactly what each one wants. Guardians are harder than they were: more health, a guard to break, and a rage when nearly beaten.

Places to find

Beyond the land you have already seen, the world holds:

  • hamlets with workshops you can use, windmills, wrecked ships and beast dens
  • hollow forts and fallen castles held by hollowborn and their captains
  • sand pyramids with traps and a tomb, and frozen temples
  • under the ground, the Sunken Halls (a whole dungeon of rooms below a ruined arch), miners' camps and crawler nests
  • islands in the sky with sky shrines
  • in the other worlds: slag bastions in Cinderdeep, glowcap hollows in the Rootdark, and prism spires in the Glass Expanse

Guards wake when you come near and stay beaten once you clear a place. Blessing stones (press F) lend you a blessing for four minutes: the wind (speed), embers (stronger blows), stone (blows glance off), the spring (fast healing), the deep (fast digging) or the magpie (more loot). Each stone rests a while after it answers.

Creatures and lore

Creatures live by world, by land, by depth and by event: cinder eels only in lava, gloam hounds hunting in packs in the rootwood, glass sentinels guarding the prism fields, fogwalkers only inside the Long Fog. The bestiary in your journal (J) says where each creature lives, even before you have met it.

Lore is entirely optional. Echo stones stand by the roads of every world, and the journal keeps what you have heard. Nothing in the game needs you to read any of it.

No two worlds alike

Every world you forge from now on has a character of its own, worked out from its seed.

Three traits. One for the land, one for what lives on it, one for its sky. The forge screen shows them before you commit (press ROLL for another seed until you like what you see), your list of worlds shows them, and the menu (Esc) explains them.

Traits
LandCragged (shelves and cliffs), Gentle (low hills, wide lakes), Hollow (more caves), Rich Veins (more ore), Drowned (fens and lakes everywhere), Long Winter (the Reach spreads), Scorched (dunes, rust and ash spread), Sky-Torn (twice the islands)
LifeOld Growth (tall, close stalks), Barren (little grows), Feral (creatures hunt in packs), Quiet Days (little by day, much by night), Shield-Bearers (warded foes three times as common), Elder Beasts (now and then a creature grown old and huge, carrying more), Bountiful (more drops, bushes fruit twice as fast)
SkyLong Nights, Long Days, Storm-Wracked (the sky turns twice as often), Starlit (bright nights, falling stars), Twin Moons (never fully dark), Ember Skies (red dawns, embers on the wind), Mistbound (mist every morning)

Moods. A land is not the same all the way along. A moor may be the Emberfelt Moor, or the Burnt Moor (ash underfoot, bare hooked stalks, husks), or Lantern Meadows (flowers, glowcaps in the open, hares). The Reach has the Glass Spires and the White Quiet; the fen the Black Fen and the Reedsea; the thornwood the Bramble Deeps and the Gravel Barrens; the dunes the Bone Fields and the Glass Flats; and so on. Each mood has its own plants, its own ground and its own company, and its name shows as you cross into it.

Two new lands. Worlds forged from now on have two more lands in the mild middle of the country, between the thornwood and the fen. The Mosswood is deep green and hilly, under oaks. Moss deer graze there by day; they leave meat, hide and moss antler, and once in a long while a moonseed. The Willowmere is low and wet: reeds, still water and willows. Willow hens live there by day and leave eggs and feathers; moss deer wander in too. A stretch of each lies within a walk of home, the Mosswood on one side and the Willowmere on the other, and there is more of both far out. Each has its own ground, plants, places and moods.

The year. Three days to a season. Kindling: showers, and picked bushes fruit again fast. Highsun: long days. Emberfall: the stalks turn the colour of coals, and creatures carry more. Ashrest: snow, long nights, more abroad in them, and bushes slow to fruit. The menu shows the day and the season. Rain and snow come and go with the season.

What the weather does. In the Waking Lands the weather is felt, not only seen:

WeatherOut in it
Rainyou go a little slower and the ground is slick; creatures see a little less far; small clinging flames die quickly (a flask's strip of burning ground burns its full time), and the rain washes the flames off anyone who is burning
A thunderstormall that rain does, and it has a wind, which blows the way the rain leans: arrows and anything thrown or spat drift on it, a run with it is a little quicker and a run against it slower, and it leans on you while you are in the air. A bolt sets fire to what it strikes; it likes a tall tree, and a struck tree comes down more often than not (a lightning rod takes the bolt to earth instead)
Snowyou go slower, the ground is slick, and your breath comes back more slowly
Ashfalla little slower, and short of breath
The Long Fogcreatures see about half as far

Shelter. Under a roof, beneath a ledge, in a cave or anywhere below ground, none of it reaches you. Under a clear sky, in the arenas and in the other worlds nothing changes.

What the weather brings out. Each kind of weather has creatures that only come out in it. They are rare, one or two at a time, and they go when the sky changes.

CreatureComes withWhat it does
Puddlingrain, a thunderstormsinks into a puddle, slides under you and bursts up; it leaves your legs mired and slow
Stormcallera thunderstorma drifting bell of cloud; it marks the ground, then lightning strikes there. Step off the mark
Galewispa thunderstorma walking whirl that flings you off your feet; it wanders down the wind, and leaves feathers
Mistwraiththe Long Fogbarely there until it is beside you; its touch blinds
Rimefangsnowcircles, crouches and pounces; it leaves you stiff with cold
Dustmawashfallswims through the ground and leaps

Fire. An Ember Flask that breaks on the ground, or a little way above it, lays the strip of burning ground it always has. Broken right against a wall or under a roof, it also takes hold there, in small flames that cling to the bare faces around; they do not pass through a wall. One that bursts high in the air, with no ground close beneath it, rains burning drops that land as flames. Rain puts the small flames out about three times sooner; the strip of burning ground burns its full time.

Curios. Between the great places the road has small ones:

  • a milestone tells you how far home is, and points you at the nearest great place (it stays on your screen until you get there)
  • a Waker's Rest: a Waker of an older age carved mid-form. Study it once and you understand one kind of weapon better
  • an ember spring makes you whole and gives your wind back fast for a while, once a day
  • the Singing Stones: strike them low, middle, high, each as the next one glints. Get it right and for four minutes every chain you begin is already in time
  • something buried under turned ground, a hermit's fire with a note (and his jerky), the Ribs of something vast, a broken cart

A world made before all this keeps exactly the land it had: no traits, no moods, no curios, every hill where it was. It still gets the seasons and the weather. In the same way, a world made before the Mosswood and the Willowmere does not have them, and nothing in it moves.

A big world

The world is drawn at a wider view than before, so your Waker is smaller on the screen, walks at a steadier pace, and the lands themselves are about twice as wide: long stretches of one land before the next begins, with taller hills and deeper valleys. (Worlds made before this keep their old lands.) Creatures come out from just beyond the edge of the screen, and a little less often.

A calm pace

The game tries not to rush or crowd you. Places you find show a quiet line at the top instead of stopping the camera (only the story's own places get a moment). Big messages wait their turn instead of piling up, hints aren't repeated, and screen shake and flashes are soft. Chests near where you start hold fewer and plainer things (the best metals are found far away), world events come now and then rather than constantly, and weapon mastery grows slowly.

Playing together

Up to four people can play in one world. One of you hosts: it is their world, and they save it. It works on any internet connection: home Wi-Fi, a phone hotspot, a school or office network.

Hosting

Open your world, press Esc and choose PLAY TOGETHER. Your game shows a game code, six letters and numbers like K7P2QX. Tell it to your friends: say it, text it, anything.

You can host from Emberwake.html in a web browser (on Windows, a Mac or anything else) or from the Mac app, and friends can join from either. Keep the game open while friends play: switching to another window or tab is fine, but closing it ends the game for everyone. PLAY TOGETHER also shows how many message boards your network reached and whether a direct line is possible.

A world keeps its code from one time to the next, so friends can come back with the code they already have. NEW CODE makes a fresh one (only while nobody is in the world, since it would cut off anyone using the old one).

Joining

On the title screen choose JOIN A FRIEND, type your name and the game code, and press JOIN. A few seconds later you are standing next to your friend. Up to three friends can join with the same code.

The first time a friend visits your world they start with nothing, just like you did: an empty pack, no armour, no trinkets. What they gather, make and wear is kept on their computer for the next time they visit that world. The join screen remembers the last code you typed.

In the world together

  • How you look: friends see the look and the hat you chose for your account.
  • What you share: the land (everything anyone digs or builds), chests and stations, the creatures (the host's game runs them, so you all fight the same ones), the sky, events and bosses, explosions, and a chat (Enter).
  • Loot is everyone's own: when a creature falls, each of you nearby gets your own share. Drop something from your pack and your friends can pick it up.
  • One at a time: a chest, campfire, kiln or drying rack is used by one person at a time, so nothing gets doubled or lost. If someone else has it open, you're told who.
  • Finding each other: friends show on your map and minimap, and a small arrow at the edge of the screen points to a friend out of sight, with how far away they are. In PLAY TOGETHER, each friend has a GO TO button that takes you to them.
  • Rifts follow the host: when the host steps through, everyone goes. The guardians, the gate and the altars are the host's to wake (give the host your offering if you made it), but anyone can use a summon. Traps, the ballista and the warning bell are worked by the host's game, so they protect everyone.
  • Switching away: with friends in your world, the game keeps running when you switch to another window or minimise it, so nobody is left frozen. While you're away your Waker rests: nothing can hurt it and it doesn't get hungry, and your friends see away over your head.

How the games connect

You don't need to do anything here; this is just what happens behind the scenes.

  • The games find each other with the code through public message boards on the internet: several at once, three of them on the web's own port (443), which almost every network allows. On claude.ai they use the page itself instead.
  • Then they connect directly, which is the fastest. Most networks allow it.
  • When a network won't allow that (strict school and office networks, some phone networks and routers), the games talk through the relay: the same message boards carry the game, bundled ten times a second, squeezed small, numbered, and sent again if anything goes missing. It's a little slower, but it gets through almost anywhere a web page can.
  • If a direct line breaks in the middle of a game, the relay takes over by itself. If a direct line becomes possible later, the game switches back to it.
  • If a friend's internet drops out for a while, their game keeps trying to get back in with the same code.
  • Everything the games send each other is sealed with the code, so nobody without it can read it. The boards are free public services, so don't put secrets in the chat.

In PLAY TOGETHER you can see how each friend is connected (direct or relay) and how quick the line is, in milliseconds.

If it doesn't connect

  • Check the code: six letters and numbers, no spaces.
  • Make sure the host has opened PLAY TOGETHER in this world since starting it.
  • Make sure you both have the same version of the game. The title screen shows the version (for example version 2026.11.20), and if two versions meet, the game says so and tells you both versions.
  • "Can't reach the internet" means none of the message boards could be reached from that network.
  • Backup: USE LONG CODES INSTEAD (host) and I HAVE A LONG INVITE CODE (friend) bring back the old way: the host copies a long invite to the friend, and the friend copies a long reply back. Long codes need a direct line; they don't use the relay.
The claude.ai page and the file are separate: people playing the page on claude.ai play with each other, and people using Emberwake.html or the app play with each other. (The claude.ai page isn't allowed to reach the message boards, so it uses its own room.)

The Ashfall Trials

On the home screen, under THE ARENAS, choose THE ASHFALL TRIALS. It is a survival match for twelve: you, your friends, other people's parties, and echoes (computer players) in every empty place. A match lasts up to about fourteen minutes. The Trials have their own kit: perks you choose, amps you fit to your weapons, relic weapons found nowhere else, and two arenas. A third arena, the Wilds, is a match of its own for thirty-two (see A third arena: the Wilds).

A match, from the horn to the last ember

  1. The plinths. Everyone starts on a plinth round the Hearth, in the middle of the island. Nobody can move for ten seconds, and in those seconds you choose a perk (see below). Then the horn sounds.
  2. Hearth or wilds. The chests at the Hearth hold good weapons, and everyone can see everyone there. The wilds are safer and poorer. You start with bare fists.
  3. Scavenge. Press F at chests for weapons (the glow under a dropped weapon shows how rare it is), salves and draughts (health), ward shards and flasks (a ward that takes blows before your health does), sidearms, arrows, rations and scrap iron. Pick berries from bushes (F).
  4. Hunger. The bar under your health runs down. Well fed, you mend on your own; starving, you fade. Hold food and click to eat it, or press H.
  5. Camps. Each camp has a fire and an anvil. With a weapon in hand and enough scrap, F at the anvil reforges it into the next better weapon of the same kind.
  6. Favor. The crowd is watching. Blows struck in time, clean hits, clashes, crescendos, takedowns, finding new places, living through a night and rekindling a teammate all earn favor. When the bar fills, a sponsor's gift floats down to you: what you most need.
  7. Night. There are three days and three nights. At nightfall the names of the fallen are read out (you hear a cannon each time someone falls), it gets dark, and Hollow Ones walk the island until dawn. They drop food and scrap.
  8. The barge. Twice a match the Ember Barge sets down a supply crate. Everyone is told where, 25 seconds ahead; the strip at the top and the map (M) mark it.
  9. The feast. The two sealed chests on top of the Hearth open about six minutes in, with the best weapons on the island. Everyone is told half a minute ahead.
  10. The ashfall. It closes in from both sides and ends on the Hearth, so a match finishes where it began. Outside it you lose health, faster each time it closes.

Perks

On the plinth you are offered three perks: pick one (press Z, X or V, or click it). At each dawn you are offered three more. They last the match and show under your hotbar.

PerkWhat it does
FleetYou run a tenth faster.
Iron GutHunger comes on half as fast, and every meal mends you.
Night EyesYou see far in the dark. Hollow Ones pass you by unless you are close.
ScavengerChests give one thing more. Bushes give double.
TinkerReforging costs 1 scrap less. Your weapons take a third amp.
Second WindOnce a match, a killing blow leaves you standing at 1 health.
Crowd FavoriteYou win favor half again as fast.
AshwalkerThe ashfall (or the slag) hurts you half as much.
BloodrushA takedown gives back 30 health and all your stamina.
Steady HandsThe glint lasts longer for you. Rushing costs no tempo.
Field MedicYou rekindle teammates twice as fast. They rise with 70 health.
BrawlerYour bare fists hit far harder.
Last EmberUnder 35 health you hit a fifth harder and your tempo never fades.
QuicksilverDodging costs half the stamina.

Amps

An amp is a small charm you find in chests, crates and gifts. Hold it and click and it is fitted to the weapon you held last. A weapon takes two amps (three if you are a Tinker). The pips beside a weapon in your hotbar show what it carries, and a weapon keeps its amps when it is dropped: take one from a fallen rival and you take theirs.

AmpWhat it does
SearBlows struck in time set the foe alight.
RimeClean blows chill: the foe is slowed.
LeechCrisp blows give back 3 health.
ReachA sixth more reach.
WeightBlows throw foes further and break guards faster. Swings are a little slower.
QuickenSwings come a tenth faster.
EchoEvery third blow in time lands again a moment later.
ThornA clash hurts whoever you turned aside.
KindleYour embers of tempo do not fade.
VenomClean blows poison.

Most amps only work for blows struck in time or clean: they reward the same play the rest of the game does.

Relics

Six weapons exist only in the Trials, one for each kind, and only in the feast, the barge's crates and sponsors' gifts. Each is a little stronger than the best ordinary weapon of its kind and comes with two amps already in it: Embertongue (blade: Sear, Kindle), Longwatch (pike: Reach, Weight), the Whispers (fangs: Venom, Leech), the Anvil's Answer (maul: Weight, Thorn), Widow's String (bow: Echo, Quicken) and Stormcoil (chain: Quicken, Sear).

Two arenas

  • THE ASHEN ISLE: the island described above. The ashfall closes from both sides.
  • EMBER PEAK: a mountain with the Hearth on its summit. There is no ashfall here: slag rises from below, so the fight climbs. There are no tunnels to hide in.

Choose one, or EITHER for a surprise (in a lobby the leader chooses).

When you fall you drop everything you carried and can watch the others (A / D to switch). Tab shows who is left.

Fights use the same rules as everywhere else: strike on the glint, never mash (see How to play: Fighting). Blows do less damage in the Trials than in the world, so a fight lasts long enough to be won by timing.

A third arena: the Wilds

On the Trials screen, in the ARENA row, choose WILDS. It opens the Wilds' own screen, THE WILDS (BACK returns you to the Trials). It is the Ashfall played another way: no plinths, no horn, no kit. Thirty-two of you fall out of the sky, each over a different stretch of an island 3,500 paces wide, with caves beneath it. Steer your canopy with A / D and hold S to dive. You land with nothing. Echoes fill the empty places, and they land with nothing too.

Gather, dig, make something sharp, find someone you trust, and outlast everyone else. The last Waker standing wins, or the last pact. You fight by the beat here as everywhere. When you fall you drop everything you carry, and can watch the others (A / D to switch). Tab shows who is left, M the island. There is no weather in the Wilds.

  • You make what you fight with. Your pack (E), the recipe book (B) and knapping (K) work as they do in a world. Gather sticks, pebbles, berries, grass and reeds as you walk, and hit trees for logs. A Stone Club or a Flint Spear is enough to win with. Most places have a workbench; a few have a bloomery and an anvil, for copper, bronze and iron from ore you dug yourself. Better metal helps without deciding the fight. Bows need arrows, and you make those too.
  • Chests (F) are few and plain: sticks and fibre, a little ore, food, perhaps an Ember Salve or a Ward Shard. A weapon is rare and never a great one.
  • Dig anywhere: with your hands through soil, with a pick through rock. Under the island are winding caves and places with names: the Hollow Forge, the Underlake, the Bone Cathedral, the Crystal Heart, the Glowcap Garden and the Ember Brink. The good ore is there, and so are things that live there. Don't go too far: about 145 paces down the rock begins to burn you, and at about 170 is the molten sea.
  • The border closes in from both sides, but it waits for people to fall, not for the clock. The line under the strip at the top says how many must be left before it stirs (with 32: 24, 16, 10, 6, 3 and 2). You get a warning of 40 seconds. If nobody falls for five minutes, it stirs anyway.
  • Pacts. Stand close to another Waker or an echo and press P to offer a pact; P accepts one offered to you. You can't hurt each other, you see each other on the map, and you can win together. Press P twice to leave it, or choose LEAVE PACT in the menu (Esc). On a phone, the PACT button does what P does.
  • The games. Beasts roam by day and hunt by night. A parcel may come down on a chute when you make your first weapon, take someone down or nearly die. When half have fallen, the Feast is laid at the Crown in the middle of the island. Whoever has taken down the most (three or more) is the Marked One, for all to see. Wildfire and poison fog take a stretch of the safe ground for a while. The hounds are let loose when only a few are left.
  • The echoes gather, dig, make their own weapons, hide and make pacts, as you do. They find a real way to what they want: up to it, down to it, round what is in between. Where there is no way they dig one. They never plan a way into the burning rock.

What a match pays. Nothing you own is ever carried into a match. What you earn is for show, and it is saved with your account.

  • Souls: one for every Waker or echo you take down. On the SOUL WHEEL page, ten souls turn the wheel, which gives you a skin or a hat you don't own.
  • Coins: a hundred for a win. Spend them on the SHOP page, where you also put on what you own.
  • Trials matches pay souls and coins too.
  • A RANKED match against other people moves your ELO, and with it your rank: ASH, EMBER, CINDER, FLAME, CROWN. Every match adds to your pass level, which gives you a title.

Ways to play the Wilds: SOLO (you and thirty-one echoes, right away), HOST (a lobby and a game code for a party of up to eight; echoes fill the rest) and, on claude.ai, ONLINE. A Wilds code and a Trials code are different kinds, and a Wilds lobby never mixes with a Trials lobby: the join screen says which kind a code is.

Teams

Choose SOLO, DUOS or TRIOS before you start (in a lobby, the leader chooses; press TEAM to ask for a team number, so friends can share one or face each other). Teammates stand on neighbouring plinths, show in green, cannot hurt each other, and are listed on the left with their health.

A fallen teammate leaves an ember for 45 seconds. Stand on it and hold F for about three seconds to rekindle them: they get up with 40 health and bare fists. A team is out when nobody on it is standing. The last team standing wins together.

Parties: with your friends, against other people

A party is you and your friends, kept together on one team, in a match that has other people in it too.

  1. Choose MAKE A PARTY (HOST A LOBBY). You get a game code. Your friends pick JOIN A FRIEND on the home screen and type it. Everyone who joins this way is in your party, and the lobby shows each party as a coloured bar.
  2. Then either:
  3. press FIND AN OPEN MATCH and pick one from the list: your whole party goes with you into that lobby, and lands on one team; or
  4. set OPEN TO OTHERS: YES so that other people (and their parties) can find your lobby and come to you, and press START NOW when you have enough.

Set the team size to fit your party (DUOS for two, TRIOS for three). A party bigger than a team is split across teams that start side by side. Up to six people can share a lobby; echoes fill the rest of the twelve places.

OPEN MATCHES on the Trials screen shows every lobby that is open right now, without making a party first: pick one and you join it alone.

On claude.ai, where everyone with the page open shares a lobby by name, type the same PARTY word as your friends and you are put on one team.

Your record

When a match ends you get a title for how you played it: the Reaper (five takedowns), the Answer (blows turned aside), the Metronome (crisp blows), the Keeper of Embers (teammates rekindled), the Magpie (chests), the Edge (clean blows), the Ghost (a win without a takedown), and more. Your career (matches, wins, takedowns, best place) is kept on this computer and shown on the Trials screen.

The echoes

Echoes are the computer's Wakers, and they think.

  • They find a real way to where they are going: over a wall, across a gap, up a stair of rope bridges to a chest, round what they cannot climb. They swim only where there is a bank to climb out by, and they never plan a way through slag.
  • They run to somewhere safe, out of sight and out of reach, not just the other way. They use a salve only when no foe is near or looking.
  • They pick their fights: by their health and weapon against yours, by how many are near, by whether a teammate is close. They go for a foe who is nearly done for, and in a team they help the one who is fighting and take the same foe.
  • They leave in time when the closing ash would catch them on the walk out, and they choose the chest they can actually reach.
  • They keep the beat as well as their skill allows. A practised echo strikes on the glint, answers the openings you give it, dodges, and spends five embers on a heavy. A clumsy one still rushes some of its blows.

The FFA Arcade's echo fighters and the rivals in your world find their way to you by the same means.

Other ways to play

  • PLAY WITH ECHOES: you and eleven echoes, right away. In duos or trios the rest of your team are echoes: they stay near you, fight beside you and rekindle you.
  • PLAY ONLINE (only when the page is opened on claude.ai): everyone who has the page open and picks the same match name meets in one lobby. The first one in leads: the match starts after a short countdown, or when they press START NOW.

Parties and open matches work from the HTML file and the Mac app, on any internet connection (the relay carries it when needed, as in Playing together).

The FFA Arcade

Choose FFA ARCADE from the home screen to open ten dedicated arenas: Crystal PvP, Sword, Mace, Spear, Grappling Hook, Bow, Axe, Shield & Sword, Knockback and Random Loadout. Quick play starts with three echo bots; each mode has its own loadout, map and locally saved stats. Crystal PvP restores its arena every ten minutes. HOST PRIVATE MATCH gives friends a code to join from JOIN A FRIEND. Public online matchmaking and worldwide leaderboards are not provided by the standalone game page.

What's new

Newest first.

Two versions made into one

This version joins two that had grown apart. One had the Trials, the four worlds past the floors and fighting by the beat. The other had accounts, touch controls and weather you can feel. Now they are one game.

Kept as it was, from the entry below: the home screen, the look, fighting by the beat, the Ashfall Trials with their perks, amps and relics, parties, traits, moods, seasons, curios and the worlds past the floors.

Brought in from the other side:

  • Accounts and hats. The game opens on a sign-in board. Make an account (a name and a password, kept in this browser) and your worlds are yours alone. Worlds from before go to the first account. Pick a look and a hat, and change them later with CHANGE LOOK. See Start here: Signing in.
  • Phones and tablets. Touch controls appear by themselves: a stick, JUMP, DASH (the dodge), USE, LIGHT and HEAVY, with buttons for the pack, the map, a quick heal, the menu and chat. The beat is the same under a thumb. See Controls: On a phone or tablet.
  • You keep your run. Hold a direction through a blow or a dodge and you keep most of your pace instead of stopping dead. Hands off, you glide to a stop. A blow thrown from standing is exactly as it was.
  • Weather is felt. Rain and snow slow you in the open and make the ground slick, snow and ash steal your breath, and creatures see less far in rain and fog. A roof, a ledge or a cave shelters you from all of it.
  • A thunderstorm has a wind. It blows the way the rain leans: arrows and thrown things drift on it, and a run with it is quicker than one against it. Lightning likes a tall tree, and a struck tree often comes down.
  • Six creatures of the weather: the puddling, the stormcaller, the galewisp, the mistwraith, the rimefang and the dustmaw. Each comes out only in its own weather and goes when it does.
  • Fire clings: a flask broken against a wall or under a roof also burns there, in small moving flames, and one that bursts high in the air rains burning drops. Rain puts these small flames out sooner, and a bolt of lightning can start one. A flask's strip of burning ground is just as it was.
  • Eating takes a moment, and a blow interrupts it (you keep the food).
  • Brews. Quickstep at a cauldron, Emberheart at a Brewer's Stand, and at a Moon Cauldron the Doublesoul Draught, which calls a mirror of you to fight at your side. And a new meal, the Willow Omelet. See How to play: Eating and brews.
  • Two new lands in worlds you forge from now on: the Mosswood (deep green, oaks, moss deer) and the Willowmere (reeds, still water, willows, willow hens). Worlds made before keep their land exactly as it was.
  • Worlds you already have keep their land. A world made in the earlier version of this game (the one with accounts and hats) opens on exactly the land it was made with, its Mosswood and Willowmere included, so everything you built, dug and placed is where you left it. Such a world does not have the gates past the floors, the observatory or the other surface wonders: a world forged now has them all.
  • A third arena for the Ashfall: THE WILDS. Thirty-two fall from the sky with nothing, over an island 3,500 paces wide with caves beneath it. Dig, gather, make your weapons, make pacts. It pays souls and coins for the soul wheel and the shop, where skins and hats are won and worn. See The Ashfall Trials: A third arena.
  • Armour at the Workbench. Every piece of armour is now made at the Workbench, for fewer materials and with no anvil of its rank close by. An Armourer's Stand in an old world stays where it is.
  • FPS MODE in the menu (Esc): no particles and a barer HUD, with an aiming cross, for a cleaner and smoother view. The game stays side-on. See Controls: The menu.
  • Ropes, ladders and vines no longer snag your shoulder or catch you again when you leap off, in every world.
  • Dead bushes give a little fibre as well as sticks, in every world.
  • A frame that goes wrong no longer stops the game.
  • This version can't play with older ones, so send your friends the new files.

And new in this one: the echoes think. They find a real way to where they are going (over walls, across gaps, up to a chest above the ground, round what they cannot climb, never into slag), run to somewhere safe instead of just away, pick the fights they can win, and keep the beat as well as their skill allows. The echoes of the Wilds find their way too, and dig one where there is none. See The Ashfall Trials: The echoes.

Worlds with a character of their own, the Trials' own kit, parties, a new look

  • No two worlds alike. Every world you forge now has three traits from its seed (one for its land, one for its life, one for its sky: cragged, feral, twin moons; drowned, quiet days, long nights...). The forge screen shows them, with a ROLL button for another seed. See How to play: No two worlds alike.
  • Lands have moods. A moor may be burnt black or open meadow lit by glowcaps; the Reach has its Glass Spires and its White Quiet. Each mood has its own ground, plants, creatures and name.
  • A year of four seasons (three days each: Kindling, Highsun, Emberfall, Ashrest), with rain and snow, stalks that turn with the season, and different rules in each.
  • Curios on the road: milestones that point the way, a Waker's Rest that teaches a weapon, ember springs, the Singing Stones (a little puzzle in rhythm), buried caches, a hermit's notes, the Ribs.
  • Fighting goes further. A heavy blow on a broken guard is a SUNDER. The blow after a clash is your ANSWER. Let a charged blow go on the flash for a PERFECT RELEASE. Warded foes carry shields that turn plain blows from the front. Elder creatures in some worlds. Mashing now costs stamina too. Each kind of weapon keeps the beat its own way.
  • Damage was rebalanced. Kinds of weapon now sit in one band (the slowest hit hardest, the longest least, and none is twice another). Tools no longer out-hit swords in the late worlds: a tapped tool does half what a sword of its metal does, at every tier.
  • The Ashfall Trials have their own kit: fourteen perks (choose one on the plinth and one each dawn), ten amps to fit to your weapons, six relic weapons, a second arena (Ember Peak, where slag rises instead of ash closing), match titles and a career record.
  • Parties. Make a party with friends, then take the whole party into someone else's open match, or open yours to others. Friends land on one team. See The Ashfall Trials: Parties.
  • A new look. Fires, pods, embers and blades glow. Each land, mood, season and kind of weather tints the air. Mist in the morning. Every world has its own stars and constellations, stars fall, the low sun throws rays, some worlds have a second moon. Your Waker trails embers at a run, brighter in tempo; a blow in time leaves a gold trail, a crisp one a white one, a rushed one a dull one; the view jolts with a hit. FX: PLAIN in the menu turns the costly parts off.
  • Worlds made before this keep their land exactly as it was (no traits, moods or curios), and get the seasons, the weather and the new look. This version can't play with older ones, so send your friends the new files.

Fighting by the beat, the Ashfall Trials, four new worlds, a new home screen

  • Fighting was rebuilt around timing. Your weapon glints after each blow: strike on the glint and the chain goes on; strike before it and the blow is RUSHED (weak, slow, open). Blows in time build tempo (five embers), which a heavy blow spends, up to a CRESCENDO. Clean hits (the sweet spot of each weapon), CLASHES (your swing meeting theirs), guards that BREAK, and being CAUGHT in your wind-up all matter now. Mashing the button loses to a steady hand, and holding it down no longer attacks. Echoes and rivals fight by the same rules. See How to play: Fighting.
  • The battle royale is now the Ashfall Trials: a survival match of up to fourteen minutes. Plinths round the Hearth and a horn; hunger and berries; scrap and camp anvils; the crowd's favor and sponsor gifts; three nights with Hollow Ones and the roll of the fallen; two supply drops; a feast; and the ashfall closing on the Hearth. Play solo, duos or trios, and rekindle a fallen teammate.
  • Four new worlds past the three floors: the Long Winter, the Stopped Hour, the Stormhead and the Outside, each with three lands, its own danger, a better forge, its own steel and weapons, new arts, and a guardian. Every guardian's fragments forge the Dawnring, which calls the last guardian of all. The story now has an ending.
  • The surface matters: sunstone by day, skyiron from craters, sunbloom and moonpetal, skyfeathers, sun shrines, observatories, thunderstorms, lightning rods and storm glass. The four gates are all above ground.
  • Guardians are harder to wake and harder to beat: each offering needs things from several worlds and from the surface; guardians have more health, a guard, and a rage. Lands are wider, and forts and castles are rarer.
  • A new home screen: three boards (ALONE, WITH FRIENDS, THE ARENAS), a CONTINUE button for your last world, sound, difficulty and controls on the front page, and HOW TO PLAY.
  • The FFA Arcade has ten combat modes, each with its own arena, weapon kit and saved stats. Quick play starts with three echo bots; private matches use a join code. Crystal PvP resets its arena every ten minutes.
  • Playing together is steadier: when two players change the same spot at the same moment the host now settles it for everyone (this was the cause of worlds drifting apart); friends see a guardian's lightning and fire pillars. This version can't play with older ones, so send your friends the new files.

Benches, trinkets, guardians and a bigger world

  • Ten benches, each with one job: the Workbench, a new Carpenter's Table, the Anvil, a new Armourer's Stand, a new Tinker's Table, a new Jeweller's Bench, a new Hearth Oven, the Cauldron, a new Offering Altar and the Mason's Bench, plus the workshops for materials. Crafting by hand from your pack is still there.
  • The recipe book (B): every bench, what it is for, how to build it and everything it makes. Every item says where it is made, and long bench lists have SHOW and CAN MAKE buttons.
  • About 90 new things to make: trinkets, meals, furniture, storage, traps, lamps, gadgets and building blocks.
  • Trinkets you wear in trinket slots (two to start, up to six), and meals that give a boon for a few minutes.
  • Things to place that do something: beds that rest you (cosy with a table, a chair and a light), planters, beehives, fountains, braziers, crates, barrels and strongboxes, signposts on your map, a weapon rack, spike traps, snares, the ember ballista and a warning bell.
  • The guardians need offerings. No guardian wakes by chance any more: each needs an offering made at the Offering Altar from things you gather and a sigil or relic from the guardian before it. The Iron Anvil needs a Warden's Sigil. Each guardian leaves a trophy trinket, and the first four open trinket slots. The Pale Shepherd only walks an Ember Moon you called.
  • Fighting styles you learn. Each weapon family starts with its basics and teaches you more forms as you use it (FOOTWORK, FLOW, MASTERY). Attacks set each other up: sweeps knock down for a CRUSH, launches for a JUGGLE and a SPIKE, lunges open a foe for a BREAK, thrusts SKEWER a held foe, and light blows build RHYTHM. A perfect dodge opens four different counters, and the better weapons hide arts that you unlock by using them (hold the right mouse button).
  • A bigger world: a wider view so your Waker is smaller on screen, a steadier walking pace, lands about twice as wide with taller hills, and creatures that come from beyond the edge of the screen. Worlds made before keep their old lands.
  • Playing together: friends start with nothing on their first visit; hosting from Emberwake.html in a browser works as well as from the app (the game keeps the connection alive in a background tab, and catches up if the browser slows it); the title screen shows the version, and the game says clearly when two versions meet. This version can't play with older ones, so send your friends the new file.

A tidy folder

  • Everything is in one folder: the app, the HTML file, this guide, and Source with the game's code in clearly named parts.
  • This guide, with pictures, replaces the long README.
  • One command builds everything from the source (see Source/README.md), and the tests now run on any computer.

Playing together, anywhere

  • Works on any internet connection: more message boards (three on the web's own port), and the relay when a network won't allow a direct line. It switches over by itself if a line breaks, and back again when a direct line comes up.
  • A friend whose internet drops out gets back in by themselves.
  • A world keeps its game code from one time to the next, and the join screen remembers the last code.
  • GO TO a friend, friends on the map and minimap, and arrows at the screen edge pointing to friends out of sight.
  • PLAY TOGETHER shows how each friend is connected and how quick the line is.
  • The world keeps running when someone switches to another window, and their Waker rests safely meanwhile (the Mac app keeps running when hidden too).
  • Fixes: doors no longer shut on a friend standing in them; explosions hurt everyone nearby and hit creatures once; a newly placed campfire or kiln is the same for everyone; chests and fires are used one person at a time, so nothing is doubled or lost; a friend joining while others moved no longer sees a frozen, nameless Waker; closing the window tells friends at once.

Game codes, easier packs and crafting

  • Game codes: six letters and numbers instead of long codes to copy back and forth (the long codes are still there as a backup).
  • Taking things out of your pack works properly: drag stacks, drag one out to drop it, shift-click between the hotbar and the pack, G to drop; chests have TAKE ALL and STORE ALL.
  • Crafting: SIMPLE: click what you want and it's made, with each ingredient shown as what you have against what it needs. The station games are still there as HANDS-ON.
  • A calmer pace: fewer and quieter messages, softer screen shake, plainer chests near the start, and slower mastery.

The Ashfall

  • A battle royale on its own island: leap from the Ember Barge, loot chests, outlast the closing ashfall. Play with echoes, with friends by game code, or online on claude.ai.

Before that

  • The other worlds (Cinderdeep, the Rootdark, the Glass Expanse) with their guardians, weathers and keys.
  • Places to find: hamlets, forts, castles, pyramids, temples, the Sunken Halls and more.
  • Playing together with friends (first with long invite codes).
  • The Mac app.
  • Simple controls and the difficulty settings.
Open Emberwake.app or Emberwake.html to play.
